methodological_rigor.justification: This is a retrospective two-center cohort of 119 de novo FL and 16 tFL patients with reasonable follow-up and multivariate Cox models that include FLIPI (Section 3.5, Supplemental Table S1). However, several methodological weaknesses limit rigor: no a priori power calculation is reported, the TMB cutoff (2.55 mut/Mb) was derived from the same dataset using maximally selected rank statistics against PFS without an independent validation cohort, creating substantial risk of optimistic bias — a particular concern given that only 14.3% of patients fall in the low-TMB group (Section 3.5). Multiplicity correction across the many clinical/molecular comparisons in Figure 1 and Supplemental Figures is not explicitly described beyond Bonferroni within Dunn's post hoc; sensitivity analyses around the cutoff are limited despite the authors noting that single variants shift TMB by ~0.8 mut/Mb (Discussion). The authors do address proportional hazards assumption and acknowledge targeted-panel limitations, but the tFL subgroup (n=16) is underpowered for survival inference as the authors concede.

clinical_relevance_loe.justification: The design is an individual retrospective cohort study with prognostic biomarker evaluation, mapping to Oxford LoE 2b. The question is clinically important — identifying POD24 patients in FL remains an unmet need (Section 1) — and endpoints (PFS, LSS, OS, POD24) are patient-relevant. Translational relevance is plausible but not demonstrated: the panel-based TMB is clinically feasible and the authors speculate on ICI priming strategies, but without external validation and with only 14.3% of patients in the actionable low-TMB group, direct clinical adoption is premature. The work informs risk-stratification research but is unlikely to change guidelines in its current form.

reporting_quality.justification: REMARK is the appropriate checklist for a prognostic biomarker study. Reporting is reasonable for assay details, variant filtering, cutoff derivation, and multivariate modelling (Sections 2.4–2.6, 3.5), and clinical characteristics are tabulated (Table 1, Table 2). Gaps against REMARK include: no explicit patient-flow/REMARK diagram, no pre-specification of the TMB cutoff or primary endpoint, limited reporting of handling of missing clinical covariates, and no explicit reporting of time from biopsy to treatment or censoring details beyond definitions. No data-availability statement, repository accession, or code-sharing statement is visible in the blinded text; one reference URL is REDACTED, so the reproducibility posture appears limited.

novelty_literature.justification: The empirical finding — that higher panel-based TMB associates with better PFS/LSS/OS and lower POD24 in FL — is a meaningful extension of prior work. Prior relevant comparators are cited (Tsukamoto et al. WES study [35] reaching the opposite directional conclusion; Alliance A151303 [44]; DLBCL TMB studies [36–38]), and the authors appropriately position their work as adding to a sparse and heterogeneous evidence base in indolent lymphoma. Novelty is incremental rather than paradigm-shifting: TMB-prognosis associations are well established across solid tumors, the mechanism is standard (neoantigen hypothesis), and no new assay or framework is introduced. The relapse-paired analysis (n=25) adds modest additional novelty regarding TMB stability over time.

writing_presentation.justification: The manuscript is well organized with clear IMRaD structure, a plain-language summary preceding the structured abstract, and a discussion that engages substantively with discrepant prior findings (e.g., Tsukamoto et al., DLBCL literature). Acronyms are generally expanded on first use (FL, POD24, TMB, ICT) and the methods are specific enough to follow without supplement. Minor issues: some results subsections (3.4, 3.6) are dense with p-values that would benefit from summary tables in-text, and the limitations paragraph is brief relative to the number of methodological caveats (cutoff derivation, no validation cohort, tFL n). Overall it reads as a polished, publication-ready prognostic-biomarker paper.

key_strengths: Addresses a genuine unmet need: POD24 identification in FL where FLIPI remains the best but imperfect tool
Multivariate Cox models show TMB adds independent prognostic information beyond FLIPI across C-index/CPE/BIC/AIC (Supplemental Table S1)
Long follow-up and clinically meaningful endpoints (PFS, LSS, OS, POD24)
Thoughtful discussion engaging with discrepant WES-based findings (Tsukamoto et al.) and DLBCL literature
Paired diagnosis-relapse analysis in 25 patients adds mechanistic insight on clonal dynamics
key_concerns: Data-driven TMB cutoff (2.55 mut/Mb) selected by maxstat on PFS in the same cohort with no external validation — high risk of optimistic bias
Marked class imbalance: only 14.3% in the low-TMB group, limiting robustness of subgroup inferences
No a priori power calculation; multiplicity across numerous clinical/molecular comparisons not systematically controlled
tFL cohort (n=16) is underpowered for survival analysis as acknowledged
No visible data-availability statement, repository accession, or code sharing; REMARK-style patient-flow diagram absent
Panel-based TMB not validated in lymphoma specifically, and cutoff is close to the per-variant resolution (~0.8 mut/Mb)
chief_reviewer.rationale: Competent, well-written retrospective prognostic biomarker study with incremental novelty and clinically relevant endpoints, but limited by a within-cohort data-driven cutoff, imbalanced groups, and absence of validation — placing it in Tier 3 (specialty oncology/hematology journals) with minor revisions to tighten reporting.
